Maladaptive Strategies.value: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
I think about why the event has happened to me
push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe

Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.

Negative Appraisals.value: The world is a dangerous place
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power

vignette:
Arthur spends his shifts at the grocery store watching hands. He watches them as they place milk cartons on the conveyor belt, as they fish for credit cards, as they tap impatiently on the counter. He has come to believe that you can see a person’s intent in their hands long before you can see it in their eyes. At seventy-six, he is certain the world is a fundamentally dangerous place, and his checkout lane is a flimsy outpost on the front line. A sudden move, a hand reaching too quickly into a coat pocket, and the breath catches in his throat. He is no longer the man he once was—the capable engineer who could build and fix things—but he can still be watchful. He sees it as his only remaining duty.

The memories, when they come, are not a story but a series of silent, searing photographs. It was nearly thirty years ago, an attempt to flee a city that was strangling itself. He was driving, his wife beside him, their two friends in the back. The image that returns most often is of the makeshift checkpoint: a rusted barrel, a log dragged across the road, and the face of a boy in a mismatched uniform, no older than his own son was at the time. Arthur can recall this fact with a strange, detached numbness, as if reciting a historical detail about a stranger. He can describe the colour of the sky and the make of their sputtering car without a flicker of emotion.

But then, another memory will ambush him, and he is no longer in the fluorescent calm of the supermarket but back on that dusty road, the steering wheel vibrating violently in his hands. It is not a recollection; it is happening now. He feels the summer heat, smells the diesel fumes, and sees the sudden, blinding glint of sunlight off a rifle barrel. He sees the blossom of red on his friend’s shirt. The memory is a pure, sensory reliving of the moment his world shattered. He feels the same terror, the same paralysis, the same certainty that they are all about to die. When it recedes, he is left trembling and disoriented, the beeping of his scanner an alien sound.

After they finally made it to America, he tried to resume his life. But the man who had loved long drives through the countryside could no longer sit behind the wheel. The simple act of merging onto a highway brought the taste of metallic fear to his mouth. For years, his wife drove. After she passed, he sold her car, telling his daughter his eyesight was failing. The truth was that being in a vehicle, even as a passenger, felt like willingly placing himself back at that checkpoint. His world shrank to the radius of his bus route. This concession solidified a belief that had been growing for years: he was no longer capable of the basic tasks that defined a man.

Sleep offers no refuge. He lies in bed for hours, his body rigid, cataloguing every creak of the old house. He is convinced that to fall asleep is to abandon his post, to leave himself vulnerable. In the quiet darkness, his mind churns, endlessly replaying the event, trying to find a reason. Why them? Why did his friend die and not him? This relentless search for meaning has yielded nothing but exhaustion and a deep, corrosive loss of faith in any kind of benevolent order to the universe. He sees only chaos and random cruelty.

This bleak outlook has become a shield. On the rare occasions a customer is kind, or a neighbour’s grandchild waves to him, he feels a brief flicker of warmth. It is immediately followed by a cold panic. He pushes the feeling away, convinced that to feel good is to let his guard down, to invite another catastrophe. Happiness feels like a trap. It was after his daughter visited and saw him flinch violently when a car backfired that she insisted he seek help. Arthur has come to therapy not with any real hope, but with the profound weariness of a soldier who has been on watch for three decades. He doesn’t know if peace is possible, but he is desperate to finally be relieved of his post.
